title: Fit for you
hookLine: judge every word and act that fits you, and don't be swayed by blame (Meditations 5.3)

cards: There's always someone with notes. You start eating differently and a relative comments. You speak up at a meeting and someone rolls their eyes.

You give money to a cause and a friend calls it naive. Sometimes the critic is right, and it's worth listening. But often the right thing simply comes with a small crowd of people who'd rather you didn't.
Marcus Aurelius, whose every public act had an audience, gave himself a rule for that crowd.

teach.h: JUDGE EACH ACT AS FIT FOR YOU.
teach.b: Judge every word and act that is in line with nature, Marcus writes in book five, entry three, as fit for you.
In Stoic terms, in line with nature means in line with what a reasoning, social creature is made for: honest, fair, useful to others. That's the test, and it comes first.

teach.h: DON'T LET THE BLAME TURN YOU ASIDE.
teach.b: Then: don't let the blame or the talk of certain people that follows turn you aside. If a thing is good to do or say, don't think it beneath you. Notice the order.
Test the act first. If it passes, the critics don't get a vote.

teach.h: THEY HAVE THEIR OWN RULING MIND.
teach.b: Those people, he says, have their own ruling mind and follow their own impulses. Don't keep looking over at them. That isn't contempt.
Their mind is theirs to steer, and yours is yours.
Go straight on, he finishes, following your own nature and the common nature, because the road of both is one. What's right for you, done honestly, is also right for the whole.
This doesn't mean ignore all feedback. Elsewhere Marcus asks to be corrected, gladly, when he's wrong. A critic with a reason gets heard, and maybe changes your mind.
A critic with only disapproval doesn't get to decide what's fit for you.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use Meditations 5.3 in two steps: first test an act for fairness and honesty, then, if it passes, don't let disapproval alone turn them aside.

o: a Roman general who cared most about the crowd's praise
the Stoic emperor who tested acts, then ignored mere blame
a Greek teacher who said to follow public opinion

games.q: fit for me — tap the pairs.
p: then the blame gets no vote
your nature and the common one

he tests the act first, and elsewhere asks to be corrected when wrong.

games.q: you decide to apologize first after a family fight. a sibling says it makes you look weak. what fits Meditations 5.3?
o: test it: is it fair and true? if so, do it.
drop it, to avoid looking weak.
games.why: Marcus says judge every act in line with nature as fit for you, and don't let the talk that follows turn you aside.

practice: Think of one right thing you've held back from because of a critic, real or imagined, and test it honestly: is it fair, true, useful? If it fails, let it go.
If it passes, let the critic keep their own mind, and picture yourself doing it calmly, without needing to win them over.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who said to judge every word and act in line with nature as fit for you, and not let the blame of critics turn you aside. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'according to nature': the Stoic test Marcus applies to every word and act in 5.3.

carryVoice: Your line: fit for me. Test the act first; then the critics don't get a vote. Until tomorrow.
